studies.title: The Quaking Of The Hour
studies.meaning: The surah opens by addressing all humanity rather than the believers, and the first thing it says is that the Hour's convulsion is enormous. The second ayah does not describe the earth. It describes people: a nursing mother letting go of her infant, a pregnant woman losing her load, crowds that look intoxicated without having drunk anything. Commentators differ over whether this happens at the first blast or on the Day itself. Either way the measure is a mother's grip.
studies.historicalContext: Surah 22 is placed among the Medinan surahs, though the classical commentators note that parts of it read as Meccan and they record the disagreement rather than settling it. These opening ayat carry the argumentative pressure of the Meccan period, addressing humanity at large about resurrection. No specific occasion is reported for them. What the sources describe instead is a community newly settled in Medina still answering the question of whether the dead are raised.

keyTerms.note: A doubled root that repeats its own sound, the way the shaking repeats. The form names not a single tremor but a sustained convulsion, and this exact noun occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

The verb covers forgetting under shock rather than choosing to forget. It is used of a mind emptied by terror, which is why the image is not a mother abandoning her child but a mother who has stopped registering him.
A plural adjective for the state, not the cause. The passage grants the appearance and immediately denies the substance, so the word is doing the work of a simile without becoming one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In seventh-century Arabia an infant nursed for around two years, and a mother's milk was the only thing standing between a child and death. Wet-nursing was arranged formally, and desert families took town infants for a fee. A woman who let go of a nursing child had lost the last instinct that survives famine, raid and flight. The ayah reaches for the strongest human hold anyone in that audience knew, and shows it failing.
studies.didYouKnow: The noun used here for the Hour's quaking appears exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah. Surah 22 also addresses humanity at large, rather than the believers, four separate times, at ayat 1, 5, 49 and 73, and turns to address the believers only once, in its second-to-last ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consciousness of God is asked for before any argument is made, which sets the order: the disposition comes first and the evidence follows. The description that follows makes no threat and issues no command; it simply reports scale. By measuring the Hour against a nursing mother rather than against mountains or seas, the passage locates the enormity inside human relationship, where the reader can feel it, rather than in cosmology, where it stays abstract.

crossReferences.why: Names the same shaking of the earth and makes it the title of a whole short surah.
Describes the Hour through people scattered like moths and mountains like carded wool.
Warns in the same register that no parent will avail a child on that Day.

studies.applyIt: Watch someone hold a child today, on a bus or in a queue, and notice how automatic the grip is. Nobody has to think about it. That is the hold this passage says will open. You are not asked to feel dread about it. You are asked to let it adjust what you count as urgent for the rest of the afternoon.

studies.title: Arguing Without Knowledge
studies.meaning: Two ayat sketch a type rather than an individual: someone who disputes about God with nothing behind the dispute, and who is following something. The word for the devil he follows means stripped of every good and beyond restraint. The second ayah states the arrangement plainly. Whoever turns to such a guide will be misled by him. Then the ordinary verb for guiding is used of leading him to the Fire, which turns the word against itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan in placement, in a surah the classical commentators describe as mixed, since parts of it read as Meccan. These ayat belong to the surah's opening address to humanity at large rather than to a reported occasion. The setting is public dispute about God, which the community faced from opponents in Mecca throughout the earlier years and continued to face from visitors and delegations after the move to Medina.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning bare or smooth, used of a hill with nothing growing on it. Applied to a rebel it names one scoured clean of every good, so that nothing catches and nothing holds.
A form that implies contest rather than inquiry. The pattern names an exchange in which each side pulls against the other, so the word already says the arguing is not aimed at finding anything out.
A name for the Fire built from a verb meaning to kindle and drive fiercer. It catches the flame at the moment it is being fanned rather than a fire already settled and burning steadily.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputation was a public sport in Arabia. Tribes measured themselves by their orators, contests at the seasonal fairs were won by whoever spoke best, and a man who could not hold his ground in argument brought shame on his clan. Some of those who came to argue with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) arrived with reputations to defend rather than questions to ask. The passage separates the two motives without naming anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 22 opens the same clause three times, at ayat 3, 8 and 11, each introducing a different kind of person found among the people. Only al-Baqarah uses that opening more often. The repetition is this surah's way of sorting an audience it has just addressed as one undifferentiated crowd.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Argument itself is not condemned; the Quran argues constantly. What is named is arguing about God without knowledge, which makes the fault a matter of grounds before it is a matter of character. The second ayah then shows the cost of choosing a guide badly. Nothing is forced: the person turns to the misleader first, and only afterwards is misled. Responsibility stays with the one who chose.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same opening with the missing credentials spelled out: no knowledge, no guidance, no book.
Describes those who dispute God's signs without any warrant, and calls the habit greatly hateful.
Notes that the human being is the most contentious of creatures, arguing more than anything else.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you defend a position about religion online or at a table, and ask honestly whether you learned it or absorbed it. If you cannot name where it came from, say so out loud in the conversation. Admitting the gap once is a small thing, and it changes what the rest of the exchange is for.

studies.title: From Dust To The Living Earth
studies.meaning: An argument for resurrection built entirely from things the hearer has watched. The stages of a human being are set out in order, from dust through the drop and the clinging form to a lump, then birth, then full strength, then either death or the age at which knowledge is lost again. Then the same shape appears in the ground: still earth, water sent down, and the soil stirring, swelling and putting out pairs. Two processes, one argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan by most reckonings, though the surah is unusual in containing material from both periods and the classical sources note the mixture. The ayah opens with an address to all people rather than to believers, and it answers doubt about resurrection with observation rather than with authority. No specific occasion is reported. It sits among ayat about arguing over God without knowledge.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to hang or adhere, used of a leech and of anything that attaches. The word describes a relation to what it is attached to rather than a substance.
Literally the meanest part of a lifetime. The ayah defines it not by frailty of body but by a specific loss: knowing nothing after having known, which returns a person to where the sequence started.
A verb of shaking or trembling, used of a branch in wind. Applied to soil after rain it gives the ground a motion of its own, which is what makes the comparison with a body coming back work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both halves of the argument were things the audience had seen close up. Childbirth and infant death happened at home, and every family had watched a body change through its stages and had buried someone very old who no longer recognised them. Rain on dead ground was the year's most dramatic event, and the change in a wadi within days of it was total. Nothing in the ayah required a specialist.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest single ayat in the Quran outside the passages on debt and inheritance, and it moves through two complete life cycles without a break. Its structure is a loop: dust at the beginning, dead ground near the end, and the return of life in both. The argument is made by arrangement rather than by assertion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The case for resurrection is made from precedent rather than from power. The claim is not that God could do it but that He is observably doing something of the same kind twice over, in every pregnancy and every spring. That shifts the burden: someone who accepts the first two has already accepted the pattern. The passage also treats the loss of knowledge in old age as part of the design rather than as a failure of it.

crossReferences.why: The same sequence of stages, ending with a phrase of praise for the maker.
The dead earth stirring after rain, given directly as the sign of the reviving.
Names the same return to an age where nothing is known after knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Look at a photograph of yourself as a small child and then at your hands now. Same person, no continuous substance. The ayah builds its whole case out of that observation, which means the evidence it is asking you to weigh is available on your own phone in about thirty seconds. Take the thirty seconds.

studies.title: Because God Is The Truth
studies.meaning: These ayat supply the reason for everything before them, stacked as a run of clauses each introduced by the same particle: God is the Truth, He revives the dead, He is capable of everything, the Hour is coming beyond doubt, God raises whoever is in the graves. Then the surah returns to the disputer and itemises what he does not have. Not knowledge, not guidance, not an illuminating book. The list moves from what a person works out to what he is handed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan by the standard designation, though classical scholars record that portions of surah 22 read as Meccan and leave the disagreement open. These ayat close the long argument from human development and from the reviving earth that runs just before them. No particular occasion is reported. The setting is a community that had to answer, publicly and often, the claim that bodies once decayed could not be brought back at all.

keyTerms.note: The word means what is true, what is real, and what is rightfully due, all at once. Using it as a name makes reality itself the premise, so the claim about resurrection rests on a claim about being.
An active participle from a verb meaning to shed light. A book described this way is not something lit up by another source; it is what lets other things be seen at all.
The plural of a word for a dug place. It keeps the argument physical: not souls in an abstract elsewhere, but the specific hollows in the ground that the listeners had filled themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in Arabia was quick and plain. A body was washed, wrapped and laid in a trench cut into stony ground, often before the day was out, marked by little more than a stone. Families walked past those mounds on the way to their fields and wells. When the passage says God raises whoever is in the graves, it was pointing at ground the audience could have walked to that afternoon.
studies.didYouKnow: Two ayat here hang five separate clauses off a single particle of affirmation, one after another: God is the Truth, He revives the dead, He is capable of everything, the Hour is coming, God raises those in the graves. The grammar makes them one statement in five parts rather than five claims, so resurrection is asserted as part of a description of God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is argued from the nature of God rather than from evidence about bodies. If God is the Real and is capable without limit, then raising the dead is not an extra act requiring extra power. The passage also separates two failures in the disputer: he has neither reasoned his way to a position nor received one. Between them those cover every honest route to a conviction, which is what leaves the arguing groundless.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same objection about decayed bones by pointing back to the first creation.
Asks whether the first creation wearied God, framing resurrection as no greater task than it.
Names the same person who argues about God without knowledge, guidance or an illuminating book.

studies.applyIt: Pick one belief you hold about God and trace it back honestly. Did you work it out, did you read it, or did you simply grow up near it. None of those answers is shameful. The point of the exercise is to know which one you are standing on, so that when someone pushes, you know what is holding you up.

studies.title: Turning Aside In Contempt
studies.meaning: The posture is described before the consequence. The phrase pictures a man twisting his side away, the body language of someone who will not be spoken to, and the commentators read it as turning the neck aside, or bending the shoulder, or swaggering off. The result is then stated in two registers, disgrace in this world and burning in the next. After that comes the reason, in a single clause. What arrives is what the hands sent on ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan in placement, in a surah whose mixed character the classical commentators note. These ayat continue a portrait begun six ayat earlier and are not tied by the sources to any named individual, though some reports connect the description to particular opponents in Mecca. Where those reports differ the commentators keep the description general, and the grammar supports them: the subject is a person found among the people, not a name.

keyTerms.note: The word names the part of the body between shoulder and waist that turns first when someone refuses to listen. Folding it is a gesture, and the Quran reports the gesture instead of the attitude behind it.
Shame that others see rather than private regret. In a society organised around standing, this named the loss that mattered most, and the ayah places it in this world rather than deferring it.
A verb used of sending goods or people ahead of a caravan. Deeds are pictured as dispatched in advance to a destination the doer will reach later, so nothing needs to be added on arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans sent part of their load ahead with a forward party so it would be waiting at the next halt. Merchants thought in those terms constantly: what has gone forward, what is still with me, what will be there when I arrive. The idiom that closes this passage is commercial before it is moral, and its first listeners would have heard a shipping term rather than a metaphor about the soul.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause closing this passage, pairing what a person's hands sent forward with the statement that God is not unjust to His servants, appears three times in the Quran in almost identical wording: here, at 3:182, and at 8:51. In all three it follows a description of punishment, as though the sentence exists to forestall one particular objection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas are held together. The punishment is severe, and God is not unjust, and the second is offered not as consolation but as an argument, because the content of the punishment is the person's own record. The passage also treats bodily posture as morally legible. A turned shoulder is not merely rude; it is a refusal enacted, and the Quran takes the enactment as evidence of what is inside.

crossReferences.why: Closes a description of punishment with the same pairing of advanced deeds and divine justice.
Describes the same turned cheek and strutting walk in a father's counsel to his son.
States that God does not love the arrogant, immediately after describing hearts that deny.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own body in the next disagreement you have. Notice if your shoulder turns, if you angle away, if you start looking past the person while they finish. Do not analyse it. Just square up again and keep listening. The posture usually shifts before the mind does, and it can be moved back the same way.

studies.title: Worship On The Edge
studies.meaning: One image carries the ayah: a person worshipping at the rim, the way someone stands at the flank of an army or the lip of a trench, ready to go either way. Good fortune settles him; an ordeal spins him around. The verb chosen for that turning is the one used of a man wheeling away on his face. What is lost is named twice, this world and the next, and then named a third time simply as loss.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report a specific setting, consistently cited: men would arrive in Medina and attach themselves to the community, and if a good season followed, a healthy birth among their animals or a fair harvest, they were satisfied, and if illness or loss followed they left. The commentators give the report and then read the ayah as describing a permanent human type rather than only those particular men.

keyTerms.note: Used of the flank of an army, the lip of a hill, the margin of anything. It places the worshipper neither outside nor inside but at the boundary, where the smallest push decides direction.
A verb for a heart coming to rest, from the root used of tranquillity and of ground levelling out. Here the calm is genuine but conditional, which is precisely the problem being described.
From smelting metal to separate the pure from the dross. The word already implies that the hardship is doing something, showing what an easier season could never have shown about a person.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bedouin families lived at the mercy of a season. A good rain meant grass, milk and surviving lambs; a dry one meant moving, borrowing, or breaking up the household. Religion in that world was often tied to fortune, and gods were kept as long as they delivered. Whole clans changed allegiance after a bad year. The ayah describes something its audience had watched happen, not a hypothetical case.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 22 introduces three different people with the same opening clause, at ayat 3, 8 and 11. The first two argue about God; the third worships Him. Placing the half-hearted worshipper in the same series as the open opponent is a deliberate arrangement, and only al-Baqarah uses that particular opening more often than this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures faith by what survives loss rather than by what is professed in comfort. It does not accuse this person of lying: his contentment when things go well is real. The difficulty is that it was purchased. By naming the loss as both worlds, the ayah also observes that a conditional faith fails on its own terms, since it does not even secure the worldly outcome it was traded for.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same reversal: belief professed, then abandoned as soon as harm comes on God's account.
Shows a person calling on God through affliction and walking on as if he had never called.
Traces the same swing between despair in hardship and turning away the moment ease returns.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last stretch when things went badly for a month or more. Notice, without judging it, what happened to your prayer in that stretch: steadier, thinner, or gone. That figure tells you more than anything you can say about your faith on a good day. Keep it in mind the next time an easy season makes you confident.

studies.title: Calling On What Cannot Answer
studies.meaning: Two ayat sharpen the same point and a third answers it. First, he calls on what can neither harm him nor benefit him, and that is straying gone far. Then the sentence tightens: he calls on one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. The order matters. Not harmless, but actively costly. Two exclamations of disgust follow, aimed at the relationship rather than the man, and then the passage turns without transition to gardens.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the portrait of the worshipper standing at the edge. The commentators read the invocation described here as the older Arabian practice of appealing to intermediaries at shrines, which the Quran had been dismantling since the Meccan years. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat. They function as the argument beneath the portrait: the alternative to God is not a rival power but an absence dressed as one.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for calling out to someone, used across the Quran for supplication offered to God. Applying it here makes the two acts grammatically identical, so that only the one addressed differs.

A patron in Arabian society was a freed slave's guarantor or a weaker clan's protector, obliged to defend and to avenge. The word names a binding relationship, so the complaint concerns a protector who cannot protect.
From a root about mixing and keeping company, used of a spouse or a constant associate. It names intimacy rather than authority, so the two words together cover both kinds of dependence at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person without a patron in Arabia was in real danger. Protection was the substance of law: an unattached man could be robbed with nobody obliged to pursue it, and clients formally attached themselves to a clan for exactly this reason. Choosing a patron was a decision people made carefully, weighing wealth, reach and reliability. The ayah judges this choice on those familiar terms and finds it a bad contract.
studies.didYouKnow: The exclamation of disgust in ayah 13 is repeated inside a single ayah: what a miserable patron, what a miserable companion. That particle occurs in nine ayat across the Quran, and this is the only one that carries it twice. The doubling turns a verdict into something closer to recoil, and it is aimed at the relationship rather than at the person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not argue that the objects of this devotion are unreal; it argues that they are powerless, which is the harder claim to escape. Harm being nearer than benefit is the decisive line, since the relationship is not neutral: time and trust spent there are spent. And the abrupt turn to the gardens refuses to leave the reader inside the diagnosis. The alternative is stated rather than implied.

crossReferences.why: Compares such calling to a man stretching his hands toward water that never reaches his mouth.
States that those invoked besides God own nothing at all and cannot hear the call.
Asks who is further astray than one calling on what will not answer until the Resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Notice where your first instinct goes when something goes wrong this week: a person, a search bar, a screen, a bank balance. Do not stop using any of it. Just add one line of your own before you reach for it, addressed to God, out loud or silently. The order you do things in tells you more than the things themselves do.

studies.title: Let Him Stretch A Rope
studies.meaning: The ayah is deliberately hard, and the commentators read it in more than one way. Some take the heaven as the sky and the rope as a means of climbing up to cut off the help; others take it as the ceiling of a house and read the reaching and severing as a man choking off his own breath in fury. All agree on the challenge itself. Whatever the enraged person does, the help arrives anyway, and no scheme removes what enrages him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah follows the promise of gardens for the believers and is addressed to someone convinced that help will never come. The commentators connect it broadly to opponents waiting for the new community to fail, and to a mood that surfaced inside the community during hard years. No single occasion is reported with agreement, and the sources present the ayah as a challenge issued to a state of mind rather than to a man.

keyTerms.note: The base sense is a rope, and from it the word came to mean any means or link to something out of reach. Both senses are live here, which is part of why the image resists a single reading.
Contrivance worked quietly, the word used of traps and stratagems. Setting it against the help of God measures human ingenuity at its most determined against something it has no purchase on.
Rage that swells inside and is held in rather than released. The ayah does not say the anger will be removed; it says the scheming will not remove the thing that causes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ropes were everywhere and were twisted by hand from palm fibre. They drew water from wells, lashed loads to camels, staked tents against the wind and were let down into shafts. A rope was the ordinary answer to anything out of reach, so a man told to throw one at the sky would have felt the absurdity in his hands before he worked it out in his head.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the passages the classical commentators most openly disagree about, and their works preserve the alternatives side by side rather than resolving them. Al-Tabari lists several readings of the pronoun alone: whether the help withheld is help to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), or help to the enraged man himself. The grammar permits both, and the tradition kept both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers despair with a dare rather than with reassurance, which is unusual. It does not promise the person will feel better; it points out that his anger has no leverage on the outcome. That leaves the emotion intact and removes only the illusion of control. Read against the ayah that follows, where signs are sent down clearly and guidance is God's to give, the challenge turns into an invitation.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same refusal to despair of God's relief into a father's mouth after years of loss.
Promises a way out from where it is not expected, for whoever keeps conscious of God.
States that if God helps you none can overcome you, and if He withholds none can help.

studies.applyIt: The next time you catch yourself certain that a situation will never improve, write the certainty down as one sentence with a date on it. Then put it away. Months from now you will find either that you were right about the facts and wrong about the finality, or wrong about both. Either way you will have evidence instead of a mood.

studies.title: God Will Decide Between Them
studies.meaning: Six communities are named in a single line, believers and Jews and Sabeans and Christians and Zoroastrians and those who associate partners with God, and then one verb is given for all of them together. God will decide between them on the Day of Resurrection. The ayah does not adjudicate any of the differences it has just listed. It says who will, and when, and it closes by noting that God witnesses everything, which is the ground of the deferral.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a city where several of these communities lived within walking distance of one another and disputed openly. The Quran had already listed some of these groups earlier, in al-Baqarah, but here the list is longer and the framing is different, since no condition of salvation is attached. Classical commentators note the shift and read the ayah as setting the terms of coexistence in the meantime.

keyTerms.note: A verb for cutting cleanly between two things, used both of judicial decision and of separating cloth. It implies a verdict that divides rather than a compromise that blends the two sides.

The Persian religious community, named in the Quran only in this ayah. Its inclusion widens the list beyond the scriptural communities the earlier surahs address and beyond the Arabian setting entirely.
An intensive form covering both seeing and testifying. Ending on it makes the deferred judgement credible: it will not be reached from incomplete records, because nothing went unobserved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a town of mixed communities: Jewish tribes long settled, Christian traders passing through from Syria and Abyssinia, merchants and envoys arriving from the Persian lands to the northeast, and Arabian polytheism still practised nearby. Arguments about whose religion was true were not academic there, since they touched marriages, markets and alliances. The first audience for this list could put a face to every name in it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that names the Zoroastrians, and the only one that gathers six religious communities into a single sentence. It is also one of very few places where those who associate partners with God are placed in the same grammatical series as the scriptural communities rather than set against them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judgement is placed with God and dated to the Resurrection, which does something specific. It takes the verdict out of human hands without suggesting the differences do not matter. The ayah is not indifferent: it says the distinctions are real and will be decided, and that nobody present is the one deciding. The closing name for God then supplies a reason to trust the outcome rather than to anticipate it.

crossReferences.why: Lists four of these same communities with a condition attached, which this ayah does not repeat.
Says the differences were willed, and that the return of all is to God, who will inform them.
Sets aside argument between the communities and defers the gathering and the return to God.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose religion, or lack of one, you quietly hold against them. You do not have to change your mind about anything. Just notice that the verdict in that case is neither yours nor due yet, and let that free you to ask them one ordinary question this week, about their week rather than their beliefs.

studies.title: The Prostration Of All Things
studies.meaning: A long list is laid out and then broken. Everyone in the heavens and on earth, the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and then, where the pattern expects all people, the ayah says many of the people. The break is the point. Commentators read the prostration of inanimate things as their submission to how they were made, and the human exception as the one place where the bowing has to be chosen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, sitting between a scene of deferred judgement and a scene of two adversaries. Sun, moon and stars had been objects of devotion in parts of Arabia and across the empires bordering it, and the ayah enrols them among the worshippers rather than the worshipped. No occasion is reported. The commentators treat it as part of this surah's sustained argument about who is owed what, and by whom.

keyTerms.note: The verb for putting the forehead to the ground. Applied to stars and trees it is read as submission expressed through their nature, since a thing that cannot disobey is already doing what prostration means.
From a verb meaning to creep or move along the ground. It covers every animal that walks rather than only livestock, so the list reaches down to what nobody in the audience would have counted.
An active participle from the root for honour and generosity. The sentence sets it against the verb for shaming, so the pair frames status as something conferred and never independently held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian navigation ran on the stars, and the year was read from the sun and moon: when to travel, when to shear, when the pilgrimage season fell. Mountains marked the limits of a tribe's range and the turnings of a route. These were not scenery but the instruments people organised their lives around, and several had shrines attached to them. Listing them as worshippers rather than powers rearranged the whole map.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah carries a prostration mark in the written text, and so does ayah 77 near the end of the surah. Of the fifteen such marks in the standard text, surah 22 is the only surah that contains two. Classical scholars discussed at length whether the second belongs in the same category as the first, and recorded the disagreement without settling it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines worship broadly enough to include a mountain and then narrows it sharply for human beings. Everything else is already doing it. What distinguishes a person is that in their case it can be withheld, which is what makes their submission worth anything. The closing clause locates honour entirely with God, so refusal is not a bid for independence. It is the same dependence transferred to something that cannot honour anyone.

crossReferences.why: Says the seven heavens and all within them glorify God, though the praise is not understood.
Describes shadows bowing and every creature prostrating, without the human exception drawn here.
Names the stars and the trees as prostrating, in two words, at the head of a different list.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once today at a time you would not normally, and find one thing from this list: a tree, the moon, a bird moving along a wall. Give it thirty seconds of actual attention. The passage says it is already doing what you are asked to do. Standing beside it for half a minute is a cheap way to remember which of you has the harder job.

studies.title: Two Adversaries Before Their Lord
studies.meaning: Everything before this has been sorting people. Here the surah says out loud that there are two parties and that their quarrel is about their Lord. Then it turns to one of them. The image is precise and unusual: garments cut out for them from fire, tailored to fit, and scalding water poured down over the head. Commentators note the verb, which is the one used of cutting cloth to measure, so the punishment is fitted rather than general.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources connect this ayah to a challenge issued between champions at the battle of Badr, where three men from each side met in single combat before the armies engaged, and the report is widely cited. The commentators also record the wider reading, that the two adversaries are believers and deniers in every age, and most present both, treating the occasion as an instance rather than a limit.

keyTerms.note: A dual form used of two sides in a lawsuit. The word frames the conflict as a case awaiting a judge rather than a war awaiting a victor, which suits a surah that keeps deferring verdicts.
An intensive form of the verb for cutting cloth into pieces for a garment. The tailoring is deliberate: not fire falling on them, but fire measured and made up to their own size.
Water heated to its limit. The same three letters give words for close family and for fever, so the root carries intense heat and intense nearness together across the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clothing in Arabia was cut and sewn to the wearer, and a good garment was a form of wealth: given at weddings, offered to guests, listed in an inheritance, sometimes the most valuable thing a person owned. Cloth was held against the body before it was cut. The picture of garments tailored from fire takes the most personal possession in that world and inverts it exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for two adversaries occurs only twice in the Quran: here, and in the account of David, where two disputants climb the wall of his chamber and ask him to judge between them. The two uses sit at opposite ends of one idea, the first asking a prophet for a verdict and the second reserving the verdict for God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the sides as two adversaries makes disagreement about God a genuine dispute with stakes rather than a difference of taste. The form of the punishment carries an argument too. Fitted clothing implies measurement, and measurement implies a record, so severity here is not the same thing as excess. Read with the ayat that follow it, the passage keeps insisting that what arrives has been calculated rather than unleashed.

crossReferences.why: Dresses the guilty in garments of tar, using the same logic of clothing as a verdict.
Contains the Quran's only other pair of adversaries, brought to a prophet for judgement.
Sets the two outcomes side by side, with water like molten brass on one of them.

studies.applyIt: Pick the argument about religion you are most sure you are winning. Then, for the space of one cup of tea, put the winning aside and ask what it would mean if the verdict is not being issued by you at all. You do not have to concede anything. You only have to notice how much of the heat was about being right.

studies.title: Whenever They Try To Leave
studies.meaning: Three ayat, two of them very short, describing what the scalding water does, what waits beside it, and what happens at the exit. The last one carries the turn. The attempt to get out is described as an escape from grief rather than from heat, and it is grief the ayah names. The verb form makes the attempt repeated rather than single, so what is described is a loop, and the closing words are spoken to them as they are turned back.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the description of one of the two adversaries named just before. The commentators report no occasion for these ayat, which belong to the surah's structure rather than to an event. A long argument about resurrection has been made, and the consequence of getting it wrong is now stated at full weight, immediately before the parallel description of the other party.

keyTerms.note: The verb used of rendering fat and smelting metal to separate it out. It carries the sense of a substance reduced to liquid by heat, which is why the commentators read it plainly rather than as figure.
A plural from a root meaning to strike down or subdue. The word occurs only here in the Quran, and the commentators describe implements used to drive someone back rather than to kill.

The root means to cover over, and the same letters give words for a cloud and for covering something completely. The distress named is the kind that closes over a person rather than a pain located anywhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Metalworking was familiar in the towns. Medina had its smiths, and iron came in from Yemen and from the north. People had watched ore go liquid in a furnace and had seen a smith's implements heated until they were white. The materials in these ayat were not exotic to that audience. They were the contents of a workshop anyone could walk into, described as instruments rather than as symbols.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as maces appears only once in the Quran, in this passage. Ayah 21 is also, at four words, tied for the shortest ayah in a surah whose longest ayah runs past seventy. The compression is doing work: two ayat pass very quickly, and then the third slows down for the attempt to get out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names grief as the thing the person tries to leave, rather than pain, which is a particular claim about what suffering finally consists of. It also describes the attempt as repeated, so what is described is a state without an exit rather than a sentence with a length. Placed immediately before the parallel description of the gardens, it makes the two futures a real alternative rather than a rhetorical one.

crossReferences.why: Describes skins renewed so that the tasting continues, using the same anatomical register as this.
Repeats the pattern of being returned each time they want to come out of the fire.
Gives the mirrored description of the other party, in silk and gold rather than fire and iron.

studies.applyIt: There is nothing to do with a passage like this except let it be uncomfortable for as long as you are reading it. Do not rush to soften it, and do not dwell on it either. When you close the app, notice the first thing you feel relief about. That relief is the passage working, and it is the only response it asks for.

studies.title: Guided To Purity Of Speech
studies.meaning: The gardens are described briefly, in the familiar terms of rivers and gold and pearls and silk, and then the passage does something unexpected. It says they were guided to what is good in speech, and guided to the path of the Praised. Two guidances, both about direction rather than reward. Commentators read the good speech as the words given to them there, or as what they were guided to say in this life. Either way the final item named is not an object.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the deliberate mirror of the three ayat before it, which described the other of the two adversaries. The pairing is structural. The same opening formula about those who believe and do righteous deeds had already appeared nine ayat earlier in this surah, and here it returns with the description filled in. No occasion is reported for the passage itself.

keyTerms.note: A passive intensive: the adorning is done to them, repeatedly, by someone else. Every ornament in the ayah arrives as a gift rather than as something acquired, which is grammar doing theological work.
A word for what is pure, pleasant and sound, used of food, land and speech alike. Applied to words it means speech that is clean at the source, not merely inoffensive on the surface.
A form meaning both praised and worthy of praise. Naming the destination as a path to the Praised, rather than to a place, keeps the goal personal at the very end of a material description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Silk came overland from the east and was worth more than most people would handle in a lifetime. Gold bracelets, and pearls from the Gulf fisheries, were the wealth of rulers and the dowry of the very rich. These were not vague luxuries but recognisable, priced items. The description reaches for the top of a scale the audience knew exactly, and then stops describing objects altogether.
studies.didYouKnow: The description here is almost word for word the description in surah 35: gardens, gold bracelets, pearls, garments of silk. It is one of several passages that recur across the Quran in near-identical wording. What surah 22 adds is the pair of lines about being guided to good speech, which the parallel passage does not contain at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lists what the people of the gardens wear and then names what they were given before any of it: guidance. That order reverses the ordinary account of reward, since the guidance produced the outcome and is nevertheless mentioned last, as though it were the greater gift. Ending on a name of God rather than on a description of the place also refuses to let the gardens themselves be the point.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same gardens, bracelets, pearls and silk almost word for word in another surah.
Gives another version of the same scene, with green silk and reclining on comfortable couches.
Says their greeting there is peace, another passage describing paradise through speech.

studies.applyIt: Take one conversation today and try to leave it cleaner than you found it. Not more agreeable, cleaner. No small dig, no half-truth to make the story better, no complaint about someone absent. One conversation is enough to notice how much effort it takes, and this passage names that effort as something people are guided into rather than born with.

studies.title: The Piety Of Hearts
studies.meaning: A short sentence with a long reach. Whoever holds the symbols of God in honour, that honouring comes from the piety of the hearts, so the outward act is traced to an inward source rather than replacing it. The commentators identify the symbols primarily with the rites and offerings of the pilgrimage. The second ayah adds a timing: there are benefits in them for a fixed term, and then their place is at the Ancient House.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a surah that takes its name from the pilgrimage and contains the call to it. The passage sits among ayat describing the rites and the offerings, and it interrupts them with a statement about hearts. The classical sources report no specific occasion for these two ayat. The audience included people cut off from the sanctuary for years, for whom the rites were memory rather than practice.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to perceive or be aware. A symbol in this sense is something that makes a thing noticeable, so the word names the rites by what they do rather than by what they are.

The first word means keeping a guard between yourself and harm, and attaching it to hearts locates the whole matter inward. The construction makes the outward act evidence of the inner state rather than a substitute for it.
The adjective carries both age and release from ownership. Commentators read it as the oldest house set up for worship and as one no tyrant ever held, and they record both without choosing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage was the fixed point of the Arabian year long before it was reformed. Tribes travelled for weeks, markets ran alongside the rites, poetry was recited in competition, and feuds were suspended for the sacred months. Animals were marked for offering and travelled with the caravan, so an offering was a visible commitment made months in advance and in front of everybody who mattered.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is one of the few that contains material the classical scholars assign to both the Meccan and the Medinan periods, and opinions on individual passages differ. It also contains two places where readers prostrate during recitation, which no other surah does. The Ancient House is named with that adjective only in this surah, and twice within it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes a claim about how rites work. Honouring the symbols is not the piety; it comes from it, which means the visible act is a reading of something already present rather than a way of manufacturing it. That protects the rites from becoming mechanical without dismissing them. The second ayah then sets a limit on their usefulness in this world and points the whole movement towards one place, so the practice has a direction as well as a source.

crossReferences.why: States the point directly: neither the flesh nor the blood reaches God, but your mindfulness.
Names two of the same symbols and describes moving between them.
Names the first house appointed for people and describes it as a place of security.

studies.applyIt: Take one religious act you do on autopilot and, once this week, spend ten seconds beforehand deciding what you mean by it. Say it to yourself in a sentence. This passage says the honouring comes from somewhere inside, and ten seconds of noticing is the smallest possible way to check that anything is still there.

studies.title: The Blindness Of Hearts
studies.meaning: A question that turns into a definition. The ayah asks whether they have not travelled the land so as to have hearts that reason and ears that hear, which places understanding in two organs and makes travel the occasion for it. Then the famous correction: it is not the eyes that go blind, but the hearts inside the chests. The commentators note the added clause about the chests, which forecloses reading the heart as a metaphor for the mind alone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah follows a list of destroyed communities, ending with an image of ruined towns, stilled wells and abandoned mansions. Trade routes out of Arabia ran past several such sites, so the invitation to travel and look was not hypothetical. No specific occasion is reported. The passage is addressed to people who had walked past the evidence for years without it registering.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a camel is tethered. Reason in Arabic is the faculty that binds things together and holds a person back, which is why the Quran locates it in the heart.
The ordinary verb for losing sight, applied to an organ that does not see. Using the physical word rather than a metaphor for ignorance is what gives the sentence its force.

The clause naming where the hearts are is grammatically unnecessary, since hearts are not anywhere else. Commentators read the redundancy as emphasis, insisting the blindness is located in a person rather than in an idea.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruins were part of the landscape. The road north to Syria passed rock-cut tombs and abandoned settlements whose stories the caravans told and retold, and the road south passed dams and terraces that had failed. Merchants covered thousands of miles in a lifetime. The ayah is addressed to a travelling people and asks what all that distance actually produced, which is a pointed question to put to a merchant.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah pairs hearts with reasoning and ears with hearing, and leaves the eyes out of the first half entirely. When they arrive in the second half it is only to be dismissed. The structure sets up the correction before it is made. This is one of the clearest places where the Quran treats the heart as an organ of perception rather than of feeling.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah relocates a failure that people usually place elsewhere. Not seeing is treated as a condition of the person rather than a shortage of evidence, which means more evidence would not solve it. That is a hard claim and it is also a hopeful one, since a condition can change while a shortage of proof cannot be argued out of. And by naming the heart as what reasons, the passage refuses the split between thinking and caring that most accounts of belief assume.

crossReferences.why: Describes hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear.
Names a seal on hearts and hearing, and a covering over the sight.
Asks whether they reflect on the Quran, or whether there are locks on hearts.

studies.applyIt: Go somewhere old this month, and stand in it for ten minutes without taking a photograph. A graveyard, a ruin, a building older than your grandparents. The ayah connects travelling with understanding and then says the connection often fails. Ten minutes without documenting anything is the smallest test of whether it is failing for you.

studies.title: No Hardship In The Religion
studies.meaning: A long ayah that gathers a great deal into one sentence. The striving named is comprehensive, and the commentators read it broadly as effort in everything God asks rather than as any single activity. Then four statements follow: you were chosen, no constriction was placed on you in religion, this is the way of Abraham, and the name you carry was given before. The purpose is witness, and the closing instruction is prayer, giving and holding fast.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the last ayah of the surah. The community it addresses had recently been a persecuted minority and was now becoming something else, which is why the ayah spends its length on identity: chosen, unburdened, descended from Abraham, named. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The reference to Abraham matters in a city where several communities traced themselves to him.

keyTerms.note: A word for a tight place, used of ground so thickly grown that nothing can pass. Denying it of religion is a statement about the shape of what is asked, not about the effort involved.

keyTerms.gloss: He chose you, He gathered you
keyTerms.note: A verb of picking something out and drawing it towards yourself, used of collecting the best of a crop. The choosing is described as an act of gathering rather than of ranking.
The verb for seizing something to keep yourself from falling, as a person grips a rope on a slope. It implies both danger and a handhold, and the ayah names the handhold immediately.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names decided everything in that society. A person was known by father, clan and tribe, and those names determined who would fight for you and who would marry your daughters. Converts often lost theirs when families disowned them. Telling this community that they had been given a name, and that the name came from outside every clan, offered a belonging that no household could withdraw.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about the naming is grammatically ambiguous, and the commentators divide over whether the one who named them is God or Abraham. Both readings are old and both are recorded without a winner being declared. The ayah also closes the surah on two divine descriptions in a row, an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper, which is how several Medinan surahs end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts a demand and a reassurance in the same breath, and the order matters. Strive as striving is due, then immediately: no constriction has been placed on you. What is asked is described as maximal in intensity and moderate in shape, which are different things and are often confused. The clause about being witnesses then turns the community outward. Its standing is not a private possession but a position held in relation to everyone else.

crossReferences.why: Names the same role of witness and gives it as the reason for a middle community.
States the same principle from the other side: no soul is burdened beyond capacity.
Uses the same verb about gripping, there of holding to God's rope together.

studies.applyIt: Look at the one religious practice you have quietly decided you are bad at, and check whether the version you are measuring yourself against is the one actually asked for. This ayah puts maximum effort and no constriction in the same sentence. Most people carry a private standard that is neither, and simply naming it is worth an evening.
